reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: Describes herniation of the subarachnoid space into the sella turcica, flattening the pituitary against the sellar floor so the fossa appears empty on imaging
The primary form arises without prior pituitary pathology, often in association with a defective diaphragma sellae, obesity, raised intracranial pressure, and multiparity
The secondary form follows pituitary infarction, surgery, radiotherapy, or regression of a previous pituitary lesion
It is frequently an incidental imaging finding in patients with normal pituitary function and no symptoms
When symptomatic, presentations include headache, and less commonly variable degrees of hypopituitarism or mild hyperprolactinaemia from stalk effect
Visual disturbance can occur if the optic chiasm herniates into the sella, though this is uncommon
Endocrine evaluation is warranted to detect any anterior pituitary hormone deficiency needing replacement
Most patients require reassurance and monitoring rather than intervention, with treatment directed at any documented hormonal deficit
reference.pathophysiology: Empty sella syndrome develops when cerebrospinal fluid extends into the sella turcica, usually through an incompetent diaphragma sellae, transmitting CSF pulsation that compresses and flattens the pituitary gland against the floor of the fossa. In the primary form this occurs without an antecedent lesion and may be favoured by conditions that raise intracranial pressure. In the secondary form, loss of pituitary volume after infarction, surgery, radiotherapy, or tumour regression leaves the sella partially empty. Although residual pituitary tissue commonly maintains normal function, stretching or distortion of the gland and stalk can occasionally impair hormone secretion or mildly elevate prolactin.
additionalDifferentials: Cystic pituitary lesions (e.g. Rathke cleft cyst)
Arachnoid cyst of the sellar region
Hypopituitarism from other structural or infiltrative causes
additionalInvestigations: Pituitary MRI to confirm the empty or partially empty sella and assess the stalk and chiasm
Baseline anterior pituitary hormone panel (thyroid, adrenal, gonadal axes, IGF-1, prolactin)
Dynamic testing where partial hormone deficiency is suspected
Visual field assessment if chiasmal involvement is suggested
Evaluation for raised intracranial pressure when clinically indicated
redFlags: Visual field loss suggesting optic chiasm herniation or compression
Features of adrenal or thyroid hormone deficiency requiring prompt replacement
CSF rhinorrhoea, which can rarely complicate the condition and risks meningitis
Symptoms of raised intracranial pressure needing further evaluation
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally benign; many patients have normal pituitary function and need only reassurance, while those with hormonal deficiency do well with appropriate replacement and periodic monitoring.
pitfalls: Assuming an empty sella always implies hypopituitarism and over-investigating asymptomatic patients
Conversely, failing to test pituitary function and missing a treatable deficiency
Overlooking secondary causes such as prior pituitary infarction or surgery
Attributing unrelated headaches solely to the empty sella
Not recognising rare chiasmal or CSF-leak complications
